newsitem.title: USA: House OKs campaign finance fund bill after revolt.
newsitem.headline: House OKs campaign finance fund bill after revolt.

text.p: The House of Representatives on Friday voted to spend millions of dollars to investigate possible White House fund-raising abuses as Speaker Newt Gingrich struggled to dampen a still-smoldering revolt by conservatives in his own party.

Eleven Republican conservatives blocked action on Thursday night but relented on Friday, allowing the House to pass a stitched-together compromise granting at least $3.8 million to probe Clinton administration campaign finances.
The bill, which passed 213-179, was also supposed to freeze funds for most congressional committees for 30 days.

But one of those who blocked the original bill voted against the compromise at the last minute, saying he had been "misled intentionally" into believing it limted funding, while it actually allowed an increase.
"We believed we were going to vote on a freeze at last year's level ... what we voted instead was a sleight-of-hand," said Wisconsin Republican Rep. Mark Neumann.

The rebels never opposed the campaign finance probe. They resisted the original bill to protest a 14 percent increase in overall committee funding and send a wake-up call about the need to balance the budget and cut taxes.

Issuing a public challenge, some of the group held a news conference to announce they would not blindly follow Gingrich and decried what they termed a "growing malaise" among House Republican leaders. They said the party seemed unable to recoup from a tough 1996 election that cut their House majority.

Arizona Republican Rep. Matt Salmon said he told Gingrich, "I have played sports, I can't remember ever scoring touchdowns when you don't play offense. Frankly, going down in a foxhole does not make you win wars."
The brouhaha appeared to be the beginning of more vocal opposition by Republicans, angry that Gingrich seems willing to delay a promised tax cut and frustrated by a slow House pace.

The speaker is still trying to recover politically from a House vote earlier this year to reprimand him for ethics abuses. He tried to fight back, giving a speech to underscore his commitment to tax cuts and defending his leadership.
"I was told for several months there was too much centralized control, there was too much ...leadership dictating," Gingrich said.
"I think we are beginning to go down the right road. I think the people will be very pleased by summer," he said.
While Republicans were feuding among themselves, Democrats united to attack the investigation as a partisan witch hunt aimed at the White House that ignored congressional abuses.

"They don't want us to look at the Congress, they don't want us to look at what they may have been doing," California Democratic Rep. Henry Waxman said. "Nothing could be more raw, nothing could be more ugly, nothing could be more partisan."

The bill includes a nearly 50 percent increase in funds for the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee, which is spearheading the investigation of possible Democratic fund-raising abuses in the 1996 campaign.

It earmarks $3.8 million for the investigation and also includes a separate $8 million fund the committee, or other committees, could dip into if needed. Democrats charge the investigation's cost could total tens of millions of dollars.

Committee Chairman Dan Burton, a conservative Indiana Republican, said he did not expect to begin hearings for a month or more. He denied Democratic charges that he had been unfair in running the committee. Democrats have accused him of sending out subpoenas without consultation and other abuses.

He also said Republican leaders supported him after he became embroiled in a fund-raising controversy of his own this week when a Washington Post article said a former lobbyist for Pakistan had accused Burton of shaking him down for donations.
"They are all behind me 100 percent," Burton said. "I am probably going to be attacked again and again and again and again because I'm in the position I'm in."
While the Republican mavericks said they had been told the $8 million fund would be dedicatd to Burton's investigation, party leaders said that was not the case.
Senate Republicans are carrying out a separate $4.3 million investigation of possible campaign fund-raising abuses.
